name: Fatima Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashcombe Free Range, sixteen thousand laying hens in four big sheds, with fields around them so the birds can go out. I'm there at seven, walking every shed, checking water and feed lines, picking up floor eggs, and looking for any bird that's poorly. Then it's the packing room, where the eggs come in on a belt and we grade and box them. In the afternoon I do the pop-holes, the little doors the hens use to go out, and clean out wherever it's needed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and how did you start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. Before that I was home with our two for fourteen years, which was my choice and I don't regret it. When Enzo started secondary school we needed a second wage, and the egg farm is ten minutes up the lane. Mrs Hale, who owns it, was very patient with me at the start. I'm still the junior, there's plenty I don't know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hens, they're funny, each shed has its own mood. And I like that it's near home, I can be back for the kids. What wears me out is the dust, and the worry about bird flu every winter, when you have to keep them all in. My husband Luca works at the builders' merchant, and with the mortgage there's never anything spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the calculator was. My daughter Giulia uses it for her homework, and I've used it a couple of times when she showed me how. I'd say there's nothing to be scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the same. It's handy if you use it sensibly. I asked it once what a hen with a swollen eye might have, and it gave me a good list, but I still rang Mrs Hale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd do my egg-grading course this winter, which Mrs Hale will pay for, and keep working my hours. I'd try to start saving even twenty a week, after Christmas, because there's never anything left before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That one doesn't worry me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Christmas cost, in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too much, if I'm honest. Presents, the food, my mother-in-law comes for the week and Luca wants to do it properly. Last year it was about six hundred, mostly on the credit card, and we paid it off by Easter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Mrs Hale say about the swollen eye?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She said the computer was right, it was a respiratory thing, and we moved the hen to the sick pen. Then she said, but next time, ring me first. Which I think is fair.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the calculator was. My daughter uses it for homework and I've used it a couple of times, so there's nothing to be scared of.
S0.think: I think the same, it's handy if you use it sensibly. It gave me a good answer about a sick hen once, but I still rang Mrs Hale.
S0.do: Takes the egg-grading course this winter, paid for by the farm, and keeps working her hours. Plans to start saving twenty a week after Christmas, once the roughly six hundred pound Christmas bill is paid off.
S0.feel: Calm. It doesn't worry her at all.
S0.quote: Then she said, but next time, ring me first. Which I think is fair.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is warm and steady, and family runs through everything she says. She uses AI a little after her daughter showed her how, and is happy to keep it in its place below the farm owner's judgement. Christmas on the credit card is a yearly pattern she describes without embarrassment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young people need a chance, and if firms don't take them, families and churches have to step up. My father got his first job through a man from church. That's how it used to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's fine for me, I'm on a farm. But I worry about Giulia, she's fifteen and she wants to work in an office, in a bank or something. If they stop hiring beginners, where does she start?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Giulia about a hands-on trade as well as the office idea, hairdressing or nursing, something with people. I'd ask around at church if anyone could give her work experience next summer. For me, I'd just keep learning at the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, for Giulia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Giulia say to a hands-on trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Mum, I'm not working with chickens. And I'd laugh, because I said the same thing to my own mother. But I'd keep at it gently, because she listens more than she lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help young people get started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, with apprenticeships, yes. But not paying them to sit at home, that's not good for anyone. A young person needs to get up in the morning and be needed somewhere.

S1.say: I'd say young people need a chance, and if firms don't take them, families and churches have to step up. My father got his first job through a man from church.
S1.think: I think it's fine for me, because I'm on a farm. But I worry about Giulia, who wants an office job, and where she'd start if nobody hires beginners.
S1.do: Talks to her daughter about a hands-on trade alongside office plans, such as hairdressing or nursing. Asks at church about summer work experience for her, and keeps learning at the farm.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, for her daughter.
S1.quote: A young person needs to get up in the morning and be needed somewhere.
S1.fieldNote: Her first answer to job loss is family and church, then apprenticeships, and only lastly government, which fits her traditional views. Her worry is her daughter's office ambitions. She shows patience with her teenager, recalling saying the same thing to her own mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad for people in offices, and I hope they find something. I wouldn't get into the politics online, it just makes people nasty. I'd pray for the families, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it touches us through Luca. The builders' merchant has an office with five people doing orders and invoices. If that goes to a computer, they'll want fewer people, and Luca does some of the paperwork side as well as the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Luca to make himself the yard man, the forklift, the deliveries, the bit a computer can't do. I'd ask Mrs Hale for more hours, maybe a fourth day, about two hundred more a month. And I'd use the AI tools a bit more myself, so I'm not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, closer to anxious, because it's Luca.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Luca's hours go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the kids' extras first, Enzo's swimming and Giulia's dance. Then the car, we'd get something older. The mortgage we'd keep at all costs, I'd clean houses in the evenings before we missed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for layoffs like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like blaming, really. Companies have to make money, that's how it works. But a company that lets go of a man after eighteen years without a thought, that's not right either.

S2.say: I'd say it's sad for people in offices and I hope they find something. I wouldn't get into politics online because it makes people nasty, and I'd pray for the families.
S2.think: It touches us through Luca. If the builders' merchant's office goes to a computer, they'll want fewer people, and Luca does some of the paperwork as well as the yard.
S2.do: Urges Luca to become the yard and forklift man rather than the paperwork side. Asks Mrs Hale for a fourth day, about two hundred more a month, and uses AI tools a bit more herself.
S2.feel: Uneasy, closer to anxious, because it's about Luca.
S2.quote: The mortgage we'd keep at all costs, I'd clean houses in the evenings before we missed one.
S2.fieldNote: Her worry moves straight to her husband's job, and she plans a clear order of cuts with the mortgage protected above all. She doesn't like blaming anyone, but drew a line at companies dropping long-serving staff without thought. Prayer and practical plans sit side by side for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who work hard deserve what they've earned, but this would need some fairness. Not handouts, but help for people to retrain into proper jobs. I'd say that at church and at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel safer than I ever have, because my work is with my hands. But I'd worry for the country. When people lose their pride, families fall apart, and I've seen that happen to a cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Hale to keep me on as permanent, I'm still on a yearly contract. I'd start saving properly, even fifty a week, because if hands-on work is what's left, I want to keep it. And we'd fix the mortgage if the bank allowed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe at work, but worried for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've seen that happen to a cousin. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Paolo was an engineer, good money, and he lost his job when his firm closed. He was home all day and started drinking, and his wife left after two years. He's better now, but it nearly finished him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the house price boom help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. We're not selling, and the kids will find it even harder to buy. Giulia would be paying rent until she's forty, I'd think.

S3.say: I'd say people who work hard deserve what they've earned, but this would need some fairness. Not handouts, but help for people to retrain into proper jobs.
S3.think: I'd feel safer than ever because I work with my hands. But I'd worry for the country, because when people lose their pride, families fall apart.
S3.do: Asks Mrs Hale to make her permanent instead of on a yearly contract. Saves even fifty a week and asks the bank about fixing the mortgage.
S3.feel: Uneasy. Safe at work but worried for everyone else.
S3.quote: When people lose their pride, families fall apart, and I've seen that happen to a cousin.
S3.fieldNote: Her mood eased here because physical work is spared. Her fear is about pride and family breakdown, rooted in what happened to her cousin Paolo after his engineering job ended. She balanced fairness and self-reliance carefully, rejecting handouts but backing help to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots with animals is a step too far. Hens need someone who notices when one's not right. I'd want farms to have a choice, and for people to buy eggs from farms with people on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, egg farms are already half machines, the feed lines, the belts, the grader. A robot that walks the sheds and picks up floor eggs, that's me. I think I'd be gone, and Luca's yard work too, with the warehouse robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Hale straight away if I could learn to run the machines, once I'd seen another farm doing it. I'd look at the care home in the village, though you say robots go there too. And we'd sit down and plan, I'd want a plan in the first month, not a surprise in the sixth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both of us at once, that's what frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Giulia and Enzo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, but kindly, that Mum and Dad are looking for new work and God has always looked after us. Enzo would ask if the hens will be sad. I'd say I don't know, love, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want a plan. What's in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What we can sell, what we can stop, who we can ask. Luca's brother has a bit put by and might help. And church, they've helped others, I'd swallow my pride if I had to, for the children.

S4.say: I'd say robots with animals is a step too far, because hens need someone who notices when one's not right. Farms should have a choice, and people should buy eggs from farms with people on them.
S4.think: Egg farms are already half machines, and a robot that walks the sheds and picks up floor eggs would be me. I think I'd be gone, and Luca's yard work too.
S4.do: Asks Mrs Hale to train her on the machines once another farm has shown it works. Looks at the village care home and makes a family plan in the first month, including help from Luca's brother and church.
S4.feel: Alarmed, mainly because both she and her husband would be hit at once.
S4.quote: Enzo would ask if the hens will be sad. I'd say I don't know, love, and I'd mean it.
S4.fieldNote: Her mood jumped sharply, as you'd expect, because both her farm work and her husband's yard work are exposed. She'd still learn the machines, but only after seeing another farm do it first. She would accept help from family and church before the state, and named pride as what she'd have to swallow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it's both of us. What would help is training paid by the farms or the government while you're still in work, so you're not starting from nothing. And labels on eggs saying a person looked after these hens, so people can choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but the hens can't speak up. Somebody should.

headlineQuote: Enzo would ask if the hens will be sad. I'd say I don't know, love, and I'd mean it.
portrait: Fatima Rossi is 43, two years into work as a junior on a free-range egg farm after fourteen years at home raising her children. She's married to Luca, who works at a builders' merchant, and they have a mortgage, two teenagers and nothing to spare. She uses AI a little and keeps it in its place, and she turns to family, church and apprenticeships before government. Her worry moves from her daughter's prospects to her husband's job, eases when only thinking work is hit, and becomes alarm when robots could take both her shed work and his yard work at once.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because both her egg farm job and her husband's yard work would be at risk at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training while still in work, so she isn't starting from nothing, and egg labels showing a person looked after the hens.
